paras: The attempted lynching of Jack Byrd was a failed effort to lynch a man accused of attempting to outrage a young lady in Rockingham County, Virginia, some time before February 1881. Byrd escaped, was convicted, and was received at the state penitentiary in Richmond on about February 24, 1881. The episode is known only from a single brief in the Richmond Daily Dispatch, which treated it as a passing detail in a report of his arrival at the prison.

According to the Dispatch, Byrd "barely escaped being lynched in Rockingham county for attempting to outrage a young lady." The item gives no date, place within the county, or description of the would-be lynchers, and it does not say how Byrd escaped or whether he was then in custody. Neither Byrd's race nor the young woman's name appears in the report.

Byrd was tried and sent to the penitentiary, though the court, trial date and length of sentence are not given. The Dispatch reported on February 25, 1881, that he had been received there "yesterday." The paper added that he had been convicted of the same offence twice before and would "pass the remainder of his life in prison." No report of arrests or any official inquiry into the lynching attempt appears in the coverage.

The Dispatch ran the item in its "Personal and Brief Locals" column, between notices of a sheriff delivering a convicted jail-burner and a church lantern-slide exhibition. It called Byrd "the notorious villain" and his offence "heinous," while mentioning the attempt to lynch him only as an identifying detail, without comment on those who tried to lynch him. No other white paper's account of the episode was found, and no Black-press coverage exists for this period.
